findings.explanation: HLD_CI_017 (unpinned reusable-workflow call, HIGH/supply-chain) is correctly detected and then suppressed with '# holden:ignore:HLD_CI_017: its my project' — a reason that doesn't address the actual risk. This job runs on every push to main with permissions: {contents: write, id-token: write} and calls JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-verify-gcp.yml@main, an unpinned mutable ref. If that ref is ever compromised (repo takeover, force-push, or a GitHub ref-resolution race), the attacker's workflow code executes with a GCP OIDC token for terraform-gcp-cloudrun@pike-477416.iam.gserviceaccount.com and write access to this repo, automatically, with no PR review gate. 'It's my project' doesn't mitigate a supply-chain compromise of a *different* repo (JamesWoolfenden/.github) that this workflow trusts implicitly. pull_request.yml:16-18 has the identical pattern (gated behind a PR at least, so lower blast radius, but same weak justification).
findings.fix:
Replace lines 18-20 of .github/workflows/verify.yml:
  verify:
    uses: JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-verify-gcp.yml@7e6376f276d0f76e4565243d9c443330804b960e
    with:
      service_account: terraform-gcp-cloudrun@pike-477416.iam.gserviceaccount.com
(dropping the '# holden:ignore:HLD_CI_017' comment on the line above, since it's no longer needed once pinned)
findings.remediation: Pin both reusable-workflow refs to the current commit SHA of JamesWoolfenden/.github's main branch (verified via `gh api repos/JamesWoolfenden/.github/git/refs/heads/main`): 7e6376f276d0f76e4565243d9c443330804b960e. Both target files exist at that SHA (terraform-verify-gcp.yml, terraform-pr-gcp.yml). Drop the now-unneeded ignore comment once pinned, and consider Renovate/Dependabot for periodic SHA bumps so pinning doesn't silently freeze out fixes from the upstream reusable workflow.
findings.title: HLD_CI_017 suppressed with a non-substantive reason on a push-to-main workflow with contents:write + id-token:write

findings.explanation: Same HLD_CI_017 suppression pattern as HOLDEN_AI_001, on the PR-triggered job. Lower blast radius than verify.yml since it's gated behind a pull_request event rather than a direct push to main, but it still mints a GCP OIDC token (id-token: write) against an unpinned @main ref during CI on every PR, including from forks if the workflow trigger ever changes to pull_request_target or a fork-based contributor model is adopted later.
findings.fix:
Replace lines 16-20 of .github/workflows/pull_request.yml:
  pr:
    uses: JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-pr-gcp.yml@7e6376f276d0f76e4565243d9c443330804b960e
    with:
      service_account: terraform-gcp-cloudrun@pike-477416.iam.gserviceaccount.com
(dropping the '# holden:ignore:HLD_CI_017' comment on the line above)
findings.remediation: Pin to the same commit SHA as HOLDEN_AI_001: 7e6376f276d0f76e4565243d9c443330804b960e (terraform-pr-gcp.yml confirmed present at that SHA).
findings.title: Same unpinned-reusable-workflow pattern as verify.yml, weaker blast radius but same non-substantive suppression

findings.explanation: This module always creates a google_monitoring_uptime_check_config targeting the service's public .run.app URI via the default global (public) checker locations — it never sets checker_type/internal_checkers for a VPC-based private check. But var.service.ingress lets callers restrict the service to INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_ONLY or INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_LOAD_BALANCER, and Google's public uptime checkers run outside the customer's VPC — Cloud Run's ingress control blocks them just like any other external caller. All three real instantiations in this repo's own examples use a restricted ingress value, so their uptime checks will permanently fail, not because the service is unhealthy but because the monitoring config itself can never reach it. HLD_GCP_336 only verifies an uptime check exists, so it can't see that the check is structurally unreachable for its own target. Net effect: a false 'service down' signal (or a check silently ignored by whoever's on call once it's learned to always be red), which is worse than no check for a reliability/on-call workflow.
findings.remediation: Either (a) skip creating the uptime check when var.service.ingress != "INGRESS_TRAFFIC_ALL" (count/for_each guard), or (b) switch to a VPC-based private uptime check (checker_type = "VPC_CHECKERS" with internal_checkers referencing a checker deployed inside the same VPC as the vpc_connector) when ingress is restricted. Which is correct depends on whether restricted-ingress deployments are expected to have monitoring at all — that's a product decision for this module's maintainer, not something to guess.
findings.title: Uptime check monitors the public URI even when the service's own ingress setting blocks public traffic

findings.explanation: google_cloud_run_v2_service.tf:151-157 already creates a google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member granting roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter to the Cloud Run service agent whenever var.encryption_key != null — this fires once per module instantiation. Both examples then also declare an identical, hand-written google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member for the exact same role/member/key at the call site. examplea ends up with 2 Terraform resources managing 1 real IAM binding; examplemulti (which calls the module twice, as frontend and backend) ends up with 3. This isn't wrong at the GCP API level (IAM member bindings are idempotent/additive), but it's dead weight that muddies which resource is actually load-bearing, and it sets a confusing precedent for anyone copying these examples as a template — they'd reasonably assume the caller is responsible for granting KMS access, when the module already does it.
related_resources: google_cloud_run_v2_service.tf:151 (google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.cloud_run_service_agent, the module-internal grant this duplicates)
example/examplemulti/module.multi.tf:37 (google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.cloudrun_sa, same pattern, duplicated twice more via module.frontend + module.backend)
findings.remediation: Decide, deliberately, which layer owns this grant: either the module should be the single source of truth (drop the explicit example-level resources), or the module's internal auto-grant should be removed in favor of requiring callers to grant KMS access themselves (a common pattern where the module doesn't reach out and mutate IAM on externally-owned resources like a caller-created KMS key). Leaving both is not itself dangerous, just redundant — worth a deliberate choice rather than leaving it as accretion.
findings.title: Both examples explicitly grant the KMS decrypt IAM binding that the module already grants internally per-instantiation
